```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, fig.align = "center")
EVAL <- requireNamespace("mcglm", quietly = TRUE)
HAS_BN <- requireNamespace("bnlearn", quietly = TRUE)
```

## What is being compared, and what is not

This vignette runs the standard MCGLM engine and the graph-structured engine on
the same six datasets and puts the two outputs next to each other. Before any
number appears, it is worth being explicit about what such a comparison can and
cannot show, because the two fits are not rivals estimating the same thing.

`mcglm_graph()` **contains** `mcglm()`. It fits the marginal mean and dispersion
blocks by calling `mcglm()`, extracts the standardized Pearson residuals, forms
their between-response sample covariance, and fits the graph layer to that
second-order object. The graph layer is a *second stage* on residuals; it never
revisits the mean structure.

Three consequences follow, and the tables below confirm all three empirically:

1. **The regression coefficients are identical, not merely similar.** Not
   "close to", not "within tolerance": bit-for-bit the same numbers, because
   they come from the same call. Any table comparing them is a check that the
   two-stage contract holds, not a horse race.
2. **The comparison is entirely about the between-response object.** Standard
   MCGLM summarizes it as `R(R-1)/2` unstructured correlations
   `rho`. `mcglmgraph` parametrizes it as a precision matrix and reads
   *conditional* association off it.
3. **The extra cost is the second stage only.** Everything the marginal fit
   costs is paid by both.

So the honest question is not "which fits better". It is: *given that you have
already paid for an MCGLM fit, what does the graph layer let you say that the
correlation vector does not?*

```{r libs, message = FALSE, eval = EVAL}
library(mcglmgraph)
library(mcglm)
```

## The comparison harness

Two small readers, then the fitting wrapper. `beta_of()` deliberately calls
`coef()` with no `type`, so the `mcglm_graph` method falls through to the
inherited one and both objects are read the same way.

```{r harness, eval = EVAL}
beta_of <- function(f) { cf <- coef(f); cf$Estimates[cf$Type == "beta"] }

## mcglm reports the between-response correlations as a vector in the order of
## utils::combn(R, 2); rebuild the matrix so it can sit beside mc_partial_cor().
rho_matrix <- function(rho, nm) {
  R <- length(nm); idx <- t(utils::combn(R, 2L))
  M <- diag(R); dimnames(M) <- list(nm, nm)
  M[idx] <- rho; M[idx[, 2:1]] <- rho
  M
}

## mcglm() takes the Tweedie/Poisson-Tweedie power through control_initial.
init_power <- function(lp, data, link, variance, power, Z,
                       Ntrial = NULL, covariance = NULL, offset = NULL) {
  R <- length(lp); n <- nrow(data)
  if (is.null(Ntrial))     Ntrial     <- rep(list(rep(1, n)), R)
  if (is.null(covariance)) covariance <- rep("identity", R)
  if (is.null(offset))     offset     <- rep(list(NULL), R)
  ini <- suppressMessages(mc_initial_values(
    linear_pred = lp, matrix_pred = Z, link = as.list(link),
    variance = as.list(variance), covariance = as.list(covariance),
    offset = offset, Ntrial = Ntrial, data = data))
  ini$power <- lapply(power, as.numeric)
  ini
}

## Fit the same specification with both engines and time each one.
fit_pair <- function(spec) {
  args <- c(list(linear_pred = spec$lp, matrix_pred = spec$Z,
                 data = spec$data), spec$args)
  t_m <- system.time(m <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    do.call(mcglm::mcglm, args))))[["elapsed"]]
  t_g <- system.time(g <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(do.call(
    mcglm_graph, c(list(between_graph = mc_between_graph("ggm")), args)
  ))))[["elapsed"]]
  list(name = spec$name, m = m, g = g, t_m = t_m, t_g = t_g)
}
```

The pair-level reader is where the two engines actually meet. From the standard
fit it takes the marginal correlation and its standard error; from the graph fit
it takes the partial correlation and its delta-method standard error. Same
pairs, same rows, two readings.

```{r pairtab, eval = EVAL}
pair_table <- function(p) {
  g <- p$g$graph; nm <- g$response_names
  idx <- t(utils::combn(g$R, 2L))
  smry <- summary(p$m)$Correlation
  del  <- mc_partial_cor_delta(p$g)
  rho    <- as.numeric(smry[, "Estimates"])
  rho_se <- as.numeric(smry[, "Std.error"])
  data.frame(
    pair    = paste(nm[idx[, 1]], nm[idx[, 2]], sep = "-"),
    rho     = rho,
    rho_p   = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(rho / rho_se)),
    pcor    = del$pcor,
    pcor_se = del$se,
    pcor_p  = del$p_value,
    ## how much of the marginal association survives conditioning
    shrink  = 1 - abs(del$pcor) / pmax(abs(rho), 1e-8),
    row.names = NULL, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
```

Finally, a matrix display, base graphics only, so the two covariance readings
can be shown as panels next to each other.

```{r showmat, eval = EVAL}
show_matrix <- function(M, main, digits = 2) {
  R <- nrow(M); lab <- rownames(M)
  lim <- max(abs(M))
  pal <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B"))(64)
  graphics::image(seq_len(R), seq_len(R), t(M[R:1, , drop = FALSE]),
                  col = pal, zlim = c(-lim, lim), axes = FALSE,
                  xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main, cex.main = .95)
  graphics::axis(3, at = seq_len(R), labels = lab, tick = FALSE, las = 2,
                 cex.axis = .7, line = -.8)
  graphics::axis(2, at = seq_len(R), labels = rev(lab), tick = FALSE, las = 2,
                 cex.axis = .7, line = -.8)
  for (i in seq_len(R)) for (j in seq_len(R))
    graphics::text(j, R - i + 1,
                   formatC(M[i, j], format = "f", digits = digits), cex = .7)
  invisible(NULL)
}
```

## Six specifications

The six datasets span the response types MCGLM was built for: continuous,
counts with and without an offset, a binomial proportion, and a bounded
physiological signal. The model specifications are the published ones, so the
numbers here are comparable to the analyses these datasets are known for.

```{r specs, eval = EVAL}
specs <- list()
```

**`marks` (88 x 5, continuous).** Exam scores in five mathematics subjects,
the canonical dataset of the graphical-models literature. No covariates: the
mean is an intercept per response, so the whole model *is* the dependence
structure. This is the cleanest possible test of what the two readings say.

```{r spec-marks, eval = EVAL && HAS_BN}
data(marks, package = "bnlearn"); marks <- as.data.frame(marks)
specs$marks <- list(
  name = "marks", data = marks,
  lp = lapply(names(marks), function(v) stats::reformulate("1", response = v)),
  Z  = rep(list(mc_id(marks)), 5),
  args = list(link = rep("identity", 5), variance = rep("constant", 5),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 100L, tol = 1e-5,
                                       verbose = FALSE)))
```

**`ahs` (5190 x 5, counts).** Australian Health Survey; five health-service
counts under Poisson-Tweedie with the power estimated.

```{r spec-ahs, eval = EVAL}
data(ahs, package = "mcglm"); ahs <- as.data.frame(ahs)
ahs_lp <- lapply(c("Ndoc", "Nndoc", "Nadm", "Nhosp", "Nmed"), function(v)
  stats::reformulate(c("sex", "age", "income"), response = v))
ahs_Z <- rep(list(mc_id(ahs)), 5)
specs$ahs <- list(
  name = "ahs", data = ahs, lp = ahs_lp, Z = ahs_Z,
  args = list(link = rep("log", 5), variance = rep("poisson_tweedie", 5),
              power_fixed = rep(FALSE, 5),
              control_initial = init_power(ahs_lp, ahs, rep("log", 5),
                rep("poisson_tweedie", 5), rep(1, 5), ahs_Z),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 100L, tol = 1e-5,
                                       verbose = FALSE)))
```

**`soil` (250 x 3, positive continuous).** Soil chemistry with a spatial trend
surface in the mean and an inverse covariance link.

```{r spec-soil, eval = EVAL}
data(soil, package = "mcglm"); soil <- as.data.frame(soil)
soil_lp <- lapply(c("CA", "MG", "K"), function(v) stats::reformulate(
  c("COORD.X * COORD.Y", "SAND", "SILT", "CLAY", "PHWATER"), response = v))
soil_Z <- rep(list(mc_id(soil)), 3)
specs$soil <- list(
  name = "soil", data = soil, lp = soil_lp, Z = soil_Z,
  args = list(link = rep("log", 3), variance = rep("tweedie", 3),
              power_fixed = rep(TRUE, 3), covariance = rep("inverse", 3),
              control_initial = init_power(soil_lp, soil, rep("log", 3),
                rep("tweedie", 3), rep(1.5, 3), soil_Z,
                covariance = rep("inverse", 3)),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 1000L, tuning = 0.1,
                                       verbose = FALSE, tol = 1e-3)))
```

**`Hunting` (1216 x 2, counts with offset).** Two prey types, hunting effort as
an offset, and a hunter-month random effect in the within-response block. With
`R = 2` there is exactly one candidate edge, which makes it the boundary case.

```{r spec-hunting, eval = EVAL}
data(Hunting, package = "mcglm"); Hunting <- as.data.frame(Hunting)
Hunting <- Hunting[order(Hunting$HUNTER, Hunting$MONTH), , drop = FALSE]
Hunting$HUNTER.MONTH <- factor(Hunting$HUNTER.MONTH)
hunt_Z <- rep(list(c(mc_id(Hunting),
                     mc_mixed(~ 0 + HUNTER.MONTH, data = Hunting))), 2)
hf <- OT ~ METHOD * ALT + SEX + ALT * poly(MONTH, 4)
hunt_lp <- list(hf, stats::update(hf, BD ~ .))
hunt_off <- rep(list(log(Hunting$OFFSET)), 2)
specs$Hunting <- list(
  name = "Hunting", data = Hunting, lp = hunt_lp, Z = hunt_Z,
  args = list(link = rep("log", 2), variance = rep("poisson_tweedie", 2),
              power_fixed = rep(FALSE, 2), offset = hunt_off,
              control_initial = init_power(hunt_lp, Hunting, rep("log", 2),
                rep("poisson_tweedie", 2), rep(1, 2), hunt_Z,
                offset = hunt_off),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 100L, tol = 1e-5,
                                       verbose = FALSE)))
```

**`soya` (75 x 3, mixed types).** A continuous yield, a count, and a binomial
proportion in the same model, each with its own link and variance function.

```{r spec-soya, eval = EVAL}
data(soya, package = "mcglm"); soya <- as.data.frame(soya)
soya$viable_prop <- with(soya, viablepeas / totalpeas)
soya_lp <- list(grain ~ block + factor(water) * factor(pot),
                seeds ~ block + factor(water) * factor(pot),
                viable_prop ~ block + factor(water) * factor(pot))
soya_Z <- rep(list(mc_id(soya)), 3)
soya_Nt <- list(NULL, NULL, soya$totalpeas)
specs$soya <- list(
  name = "soya", data = soya, lp = soya_lp, Z = soya_Z,
  args = list(link = c("identity", "log", "logit"),
              variance = c("constant", "tweedie", "binomialP"),
              power_fixed = rep(TRUE, 3), Ntrial = soya_Nt,
              control_initial = init_power(soya_lp, soya,
                c("identity", "log", "logit"),
                c("constant", "tweedie", "binomialP"), c(0, 1, 1),
                soya_Z, Ntrial = soya_Nt),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 100L, tol = 1e-5,
                                       verbose = FALSE)))
```

**`NewBorn` (270 x 3, physiological).** Heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen
saturation on premature newborns.

```{r spec-newborn, eval = EVAL}
data(NewBorn, package = "mcglm"); NewBorn <- as.data.frame(NewBorn)
specs$NewBorn <- list(
  name = "NewBorn", data = NewBorn,
  lp = list(HR ~ Sex + GA, RR ~ Sex + GA, SPO2 ~ Sex + GA),
  Z = rep(list(mc_id(NewBorn)), 3),
  args = list(link = c("log", "log", "identity"),
              variance = c("tweedie", "tweedie", "constant"),
              power_fixed = rep(TRUE, 3),
              control_algorithm = list(max_iter = 100L, tol = 1e-5,
                                       verbose = FALSE)))
```

## Running both engines

```{r run, eval = EVAL}
fits <- lapply(specs, fit_pair)
sels <- lapply(fits, function(p) suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  mc_graph_stepwise(p$g, criterion = "gbic", trace = FALSE))))
pts  <- lapply(fits, pair_table)
```

## The master table

```{r master, eval = EVAL}
master <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(p, sel, pt) {
  R <- p$g$graph$R
  data.frame(
    dataset   = p$name,
    n         = p$g$graph$n,
    R         = R,
    beta_gap  = max(abs(beta_of(p$m) - beta_of(p$g))),
    rho_free  = choose(R, 2),
    edges     = sel$n_edges,
    dropped   = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - sel$n_edges / choose(R, 2))),
    flips     = sum(pt$rho_p < .05 & pt$pcor_p >= .05),
    wald_p    = unname(mc_test_independence(p$g, robust = TRUE)$p.value),
    sec_mcglm = round(p$t_m, 2),
    sec_graph = round(p$t_g, 2),
    row.names = NULL, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}, fits, sels, pts))
knitr::kable(master, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2, 2))
```

Read the columns in three groups.

**`beta_gap` is exactly zero on every dataset.** This is the two-stage contract,
visible: the largest absolute discrepancy between the regression coefficients of
the two fits, across all six models and every coefficient in them, is zero. The
graph layer buys its structure without touching a single mean parameter. If you
were hoping the graph layer would sharpen the regression estimates, this column
is the answer: it does not, and it is not meant to.

**`rho_free` versus `edges`.** The standard fit always carries `R(R-1)/2`
correlation parameters; it has no mechanism to decide that one of them is
unnecessary. The graph layer, selected by GBIC, keeps between 0 and 7 of them.
`Hunting` is the extreme: the single available correlation is dropped
altogether.

**`sec_mcglm` versus `sec_graph`.** The graph timing *includes* the marginal fit,
because `mcglm_graph()` performs it internally, so the two columns are not
additive: the second is the first plus the second stage. They come out
indistinguishable, and on some runs `sec_graph` is even the smaller of the two.
That is not the graph layer running faster than nothing; it is the second stage
costing less than the run-to-run variation of the marginal fit it sits on top
of, at every sample size here including `n = 5190`. The graph layer is not where
the computation goes.

## Where the two readings disagree

The `flips` column counts the pairs that a standard analysis would call
significantly correlated and that the conditional reading does not
(`rho` significant at 5%, partial correlation not). These are exactly the
conclusions that change depending on which engine you ran.

```{r flips, eval = EVAL}
flips <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(pt, nm) {
  f <- pt[pt$rho_p < .05 & pt$pcor_p >= .05, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(f)) NULL else cbind(dataset = nm, f)
}, pts, names(pts)))
knitr::kable(flips, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Each row is a pair of responses that look associated until the other responses
are held fixed. `VECT-ANL` in `marks` is the textbook case: a marginal
correlation of 0.49, significant at 5%, that falls to 0.08 and loses all
significance once algebra is conditioned on. `Ndoc-Nhosp` in `ahs` behaves the
same way with 5190 observations, so this is not a small-sample artifact. And in
`Hunting` the single correlation between the two prey counts is significant
marginally and not conditionally, which is why GBIC keeps no edge at all.

The table is deliberately conservative: it counts only pairs that cross the
significance threshold in one reading and not in the other. `MECH-ANL` in
`marks` does not appear in it, because with `n = 88` its marginal correlation of
0.41 already fails to reach 5% on its own (`rho_p` close to 0.115), and yet its
partial correlation is `-0.002`, the largest collapse in this comparison.
"Not enough evidence of a marginal association" and "no conditional
association" are different claims, and only the second engine is in a position
to make the second one.

The `shrink` column generalizes this beyond the significance threshold: it is
the fraction of the marginal association that does *not* survive conditioning.

```{r shrink, eval = EVAL}
shr <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(pt, nm) data.frame(
  dataset = nm,
  pairs = nrow(pt),
  median_shrink = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * stats::median(pt$shrink)),
  max_shrink = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(pt$shrink)),
  marg_signif = sum(pt$rho_p < .05),
  cond_signif = sum(pt$pcor_p < .05),
  row.names = NULL), pts, names(pts)))
knitr::kable(shr, row.names = FALSE)
```

## The two matrices, side by side

`marks` shows the contrast most sharply, so it gets the full treatment: the
marginal correlation matrix that the standard fit reports, and the partial
correlation matrix the graph layer reads off the precision.

```{r marks-panels, eval = EVAL && HAS_BN, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8}
p <- fits$marks; nm <- p$g$graph$response_names
Rmarg <- rho_matrix(pts$marks$rho, nm)
Rpart <- mc_partial_cor(p$g)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 4, 4, 1))
show_matrix(Rmarg, "mcglm: marginal correlation")
show_matrix(Rpart, "mcglmgraph: partial correlation")
par(op)
```

The left panel is uniformly warm: every one of the ten pairs correlates between
0.39 and 0.71, which is the honest summary of what the standard fit found. The
right panel is where the structure appears. The `MECH`-`VECT`-`ALG` block and the
`ALG`-`ANL`-`STAT` block survive; the four cells linking `{MECH, VECT}` to
`{ANL, STAT}` collapse to roughly zero. Algebra separates the two groups.

The same fit, three matrices, in the order the package computes them:

```{r marks-matrices, eval = EVAL && HAS_BN}
round(p$g$graph$Sigma_b, 3)   # residual between-response covariance
round(p$g$graph$K_b, 3)       # precision: the parametrized object
round(Rpart, 3)               # partial correlations read off K_b
```

`K_b` is the object the GGM layer actually parametrizes, as a linear combination
of canonical bases. Its off-diagonal entries carry the conditional structure
directly, and they line up exactly with the selection: the four smallest in
magnitude are `MECH-ANL` (0.003), `VECT-STAT` (-0.038), `MECH-STAT` (-0.044) and
`VECT-ANL` (-0.157), and those four are precisely the four edges GBIC drops. The
covariance `Sigma_b` shows none of this. Its entries for the same four pairs run
from 0.385 to 0.480 against 0.541 to 0.703 for the six that are kept: the
dropped pairs are the smaller ones, but nothing there is remotely near zero, and
no threshold on `Sigma_b` separates the two groups the way the inverse does. The
difference is categorical only in `K_b`, which is why that is the object the
layer parametrizes.

## Selected structures

```{r supports, eval = EVAL}
supp <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(p, sel) {
  rn <- p$g$graph$response_names; e <- sel$edges
  data.frame(
    dataset = p$name,
    support = if (is.null(e) || !nrow(e)) "(empty)" else
      paste(apply(e, 1, function(r) paste(rn[r[1]], rn[r[2]], sep = "-")),
            collapse = ", "),
    row.names = NULL, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}, fits, sels))
knitr::kable(supp, row.names = FALSE)
```

Three of these are readable as substantive claims rather than parameter counts.
`marks` recovers the butterfly with algebra at the center. `soil` returns the
chain `CA - MG - K`: magnesium separates calcium from potassium, and the direct
`CA-K` link is not needed once it is held fixed. `NewBorn` keeps `HR-RR`, the
cardio-respiratory coupling, and drops both links to oxygen saturation.

```{r networks, eval = EVAL, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (nm in names(sels)) mc_plot_network(sels[[nm]]$fit, edge_labels = TRUE)
par(op)
```

## Parsimony, and whether it is paid for

Dropping edges is only a gain if the criterion agrees. GBIC on the saturated
graph against GBIC on the selected one:

```{r criteria, eval = EVAL}
crit <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(p, s) {
  sat <- unname(mc_compute_criterion(p$g, "gbic"))
  sel <- unname(mc_compute_criterion(s$fit, "gbic"))
  data.frame(dataset = p$name, npar_sat = p$g$graph$npar,
             npar_sel = s$fit$graph$npar, gbic_sat = sat, gbic_sel = sel,
             delta = sel - sat, row.names = NULL)
}, fits, sels))
knitr::kable(crit, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

`delta` is negative on all six: every selected structure improves GBIC over the
saturated one. The parsimony is not imposed, it is preferred.

## What the graph layer does not give you

The columns above are the gains. The limits are as follows, and they are not
small print.

* **No improvement in the mean model.** `beta_gap = 0` is not a rounding
  statement. The regression estimates, their standard errors and every inherited
  method (`vcov`, `gof`, `pAIC`, `pBIC`, `plogLik`) refer to the first-stage fit
  and are untouched.
* **The uncertainty is conditional on the estimated residuals.** The
  delta-method standard errors in `pcor_se` treat the first-stage fit as given.
  `mc_partial_cor_delta(variability = "two_stage")` propagates its uncertainty,
  and so does `mc_vcov_graph(type = "two_stage")` for the graph parameters. For
  the partial correlations, the empirical and the two-stage variances agree to
  first order when the mean is correctly specified, the conditional covariance
  of the Pearson residuals does not change with the covariates and the support
  contains the true one. With count responses the residual correlation can
  vary with the mean, the agreement is then only approximate, and the
  two-stage form is the one to report.
* **A selected support is not a tested support.** `mc_graph_stepwise()` searches,
  and the p-values reported afterwards on the selected graph are descriptive.
  Nothing here delivers post-selection inference.
* **"Conditional association" is second-order.** A missing edge means absence of
  second-order conditional association. It coincides with full conditional
  independence under joint normality, or on the latent scale of a Gaussian
  copula, not in general.
* **The graph is on residuals.** Edges describe residual conditional association
  among responses after the marginal means are removed, which is a different
  object from raw marginal association among the responses themselves.

## Summary

Across six datasets, four variance functions and sample sizes from 75 to 5190,
the comparison is consistent. The two engines return **identical** mean models,
at a second-stage cost measured in fractions of a second. What the graph layer
adds is a different reading of the same residual second-order object: partial
instead of marginal correlations, with standard errors and tests attached, a
selectable support that GBIC prefers to the saturated one on every dataset, and
in four of the six cases at least one pair whose apparent association does not
survive conditioning.

Whether that reading is the one you want is a modeling question. If the
between-response correlations are nuisance, the standard fit already gives you
everything. If they are the object of interest, the marginal correlation vector
is the wrong summary, and the rows of the `flips` table above are what it costs
to use it anyway.

## References

Bonat, W. H. and Jorgensen, B. (2016). Multivariate covariance generalized
linear models. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C*, 65(5),
649--675. <doi:10.1111/rssc.12145>

Bonat, W. H. (2018). Multiple response variables regression models in R: the
mcglm package. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 84(4), 1--30.
<doi:10.18637/jss.v084.i04>
